Simple Somos Sequence

SequencesDivisibilityInvariants
Game: Each new number is made from the two before it: square the last one, add m, and divide by the one before. Do the divisions always come out even?
How to play: Change m and the two starting numbers a and b, and watch the list.

    m a b
    Look for the math

    An old Russian olympiad problem: show that the numbers a1 = a2 = 1, an = (an−1² + 2) / an−2 are all whole: 1, 1, 3, 11, 41, 153, … Each step divides, and it is a surprise that the division is always exact. Sequences built by such divisions are named after Michael Somos (Somos sequences).

    Something that does not change

    Take three terms in a row, x, y, z. The rule says xz = y² + m. Then

    k = (x² + y² + m) / (xy)

    is the same for x, y as for y, z: an invariant. (Subtract the two versions: x² − z² must equal k y (x − z), which holds because x + z = ky.)

    No division needed

    So the rule can be rewritten as z = k y − x: multiply and subtract, no division at all. With a = b = 1, k = m + 2 is a whole number, and every term is too, for every m, as the page says. The logic test ran every m from 1 to 100 and checked the invariant term by term.

    Other starts

    Starting from other a and b, the terms stay whole exactly when the first division works (a divides b² + m) and k is a whole number; otherwise the applet raises an alarm. The test confirmed this rule on all 1,000,000 starts the controls allow.

    Try a = 1, b = 2: for which m do all the terms come out whole?

    Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
